openers.paleoarchean-era: The Paleoarchean is where life stops being a maybe. Stromatolites in the Pilbara's Dresser Formation, laid down about 3,483–3,479 million years ago, are the earliest direct evidence of life, and microbes may already have lived around hot springs on land. Meanwhile the continents were taking shape: the Wyoming and Dharwar cratons began, and the Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents. Above it all hung a stable atmosphere of nitrogen, methane and carbon dioxide, and below it, spherule layers at Barberton record giant impacts still striking.
openers.mesoarchean-era: In the Mesoarchean, Earth learned to make oxygen. Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesizers appears about 3.2 billion years ago, and a brief rise in oxygen followed around 2,980–2,960 million years ago. The planet was warm, perhaps very warm, yet it also saw the Pongola glaciation, the oldest known on Earth. Continental crust grew fast, the hypothetical supercontinent Ur may have formed, and plate tectonics may have begun, though its timing is still debated.

reviews.eoarchean-era: The Eoarchean left Earth its first lasting rock. The Acasta Gneiss and the first cratons, built of granite blocks from crust that was melted and reworked again and again, began the long work of making continents. Oceans held enough water for Isua's pillow basalts, a magnetic field shielded the air, and carbon already cycled much as it does today. In that setting, simple photosynthesis that released no oxygen appeared, and graphite at Isua and Akilia may hold the first traces of life, though every such claim is still disputed.
reviews.paleoarchean-era: The Paleoarchean turned faint hints of life into a fossil record. Stromatolites at Dresser and Strelley Pool, microfossils at Barberton and in the Fig Tree and Moodies rocks, and mats on tidal flats and around hot springs show microbes thriving in water and perhaps on land. They lived under a nitrogen-rich air with almost no oxygen, on a planet still struck by huge asteroids, such as the one that left the S2 layer. Around them, cratons like Kaapvaal, Pilbara, Zimbabwe and Dharwar grew and stabilized, possibly joining as Vaalbara.

arch-006.title: Akilia graphite and the hunt for early life
arch-006.text: A smudge of graphite on a small Greenland island set off a long argument about the first life. The graphite, in metamorphosed rock on Akilia Island, is low in carbon-13, which may mark organic matter from living things. An igneous band cutting the rock shows it is no younger than 3.85 billion years. Yet the rock's sedimentary origin, its age and its carbon have all been questioned, and the find sparked debate over photosynthetic life before 3.8 billion years ago.

arch-007.title: The East European Craton begins
arch-007.text: The ground beneath Ukraine and western Russia holds some of Europe's oldest crust. The first rocks of the Ukrainian Shield and Voronezh Massif were laid down around 3.8 billion years ago, starting the East European Craton. This Archean crust, 3.2–3.8 billion years old, lies in the craton's southwest and east. Its Sarmatian part holds Archean terranes, blocks of crust joined to the craton, of about 3.7–2.7 billion years.

arch-008.title: The first cratons, cores of the continents
arch-008.text:
Every continent today is built around an ancient, stubborn core. These cores are cratons: old, stable parts of the continental lithosphere, the rigid outer shell, with deep roots. The first complete continental masses of this kind, built of granite blocks, appeared around 3,800 million years ago, and most cratons formed in the Archean.

One of the first great continental masses began to gather on the eastern edge of the Antarctic craton, where felsic magmas rose. Antarctic zircons of 3.9–3.0 billion years suggest that recycling within the crust, melting old rock into lighter new rock, was key to building them. The work was substantial: about 39% of modern continental crust formed in the Archean.

arch-010.title: The oldest banded iron formations
arch-010.text: Rocks striped in rust and silica record a world almost without oxygen. Banded iron formations are made of thin alternating layers rich in iron and in silica, and the oldest known lie at Isua, in Greenland's greenstone belt, dating from about 3,800–3,700 million years ago. Their iron isotopes point to extremely low oxygen and to iron oxidized by {{ref:arch-013}}. Iron formations of this Algoma type formed mainly in the Archean, and deposition later peaked near the eon's end.

arch-009.title: Greenland's Isua Greenstone Belt
arch-009.text: Pillows of lava in Greenland prove there was water to erupt into. The Isua belt, built from volcanic and sedimentary layers about 3,800 and 3,700 million years old, is the largest exposure of Eoarchean supracrustal rock, rock formed at the surface, on Earth. Its pillow basalt formed in an underwater eruption, so liquid water existed 3.8 billion years ago. How the belt formed, by plate tectonics or by heat-pipe or plume volcanism, is still contentious.

arch-012.title: South China's Yangtze Block takes shape
arch-012.text: China's oldest rocks lie in the Yangtze Block. This northwestern part of the South China Craton is thought to have formed around 3.8–3.2 billion years ago. Detrital zircons, grains worn from older rock, 3.8 billion years old preserve remnants of that ancient crust. Its Kongling Complex holds the country's oldest rocks, with zircon ages of 3.3–2.9 billion years.

arch-011.title: The Pilbara Craton, a pristine Archean survivor
arch-011.text:
Only two places on Earth keep Archean crust in near-original condition, and Western Australia's Pilbara Craton is one of them. The other is South Africa's {{ref:arch-016}}. The Pilbara holds crust up to 3.8 billion years old, intruded by granite domes and greenstone belts of about 3.5–3.2 billion years.

Its story starts before its oldest rocks. Detrital zircons of 3.8–3.6 billion years show that crust was already eroding 300 million years before the oldest rocks that survive. The craton stabilized around 3,600 million years ago, as continents possibly gathered into Vaalbara. By 2.97 billion years ago the West Pilbara Terrane had collided with the East Pilbara Terrane and joined it.

arch-013.title: Photosynthesis without oxygen
arch-013.text:
The first sun-powered life gave off no oxygen at all. Anaerobic microbes, which live without oxygen, appear from about 3.7 billion years ago, among them chemotrophs that fed on chemicals and early photosynthesizers. Their simpler, anoxygenic photosynthesis used hydrogen sulfide, sulfur or iron in place of water, so it released no oxygen.

These bacteria made ATP, the cell's energy currency, from a proton gradient across a membrane, a mechanism nearly all later organisms still use. The first of them may have lived at acidic hydrothermal vents, using faint geothermal light. Geochemical evidence suggests this photosynthesis emerged 3.3–3.5 billion years ago, and fossils thought to be filamentous photosynthesizers date to 3.4 billion.

arch-014.title: Earth's magnetic field switches on
arch-014.text:
An invisible shield was already around Earth 3.7 billion years ago. Evidence from Greenland, published in 2024, shows the planet had a magnetic field by 3,700 million years ago. Earlier work on magnetism frozen into Australian lava and South African conglomerate had traced it back to at least about 3,450 million years ago.

Earth, like most planets, makes its field through the motion of electrically conducting fluids. Here that fluid is the molten outer core left by {{ref:hade-003}}. By 3.5 billion years ago its currents drove a field that helped stop the solar wind from stripping away the atmosphere.

arch-015.title: Disputed traces of life at Isua
arch-015.text:
Whether life left marks at Isua depends on whom you ask. Metasedimentary rocks about 3.7 billion years old in Greenland hold graphite whose carbon isotopes suggest sorting by living things. It is the earliest such evidence from a rock unit rather than a single mineral grain.

In 2016 a team reported dome-shaped stromatolites 1–4 cm high, 220 million years older than those of {{ref:arch-022}}. The layers sit on volcanic rock dated 3.709 billion years and beneath beds dated 3.695 billion. Then a 2018 study, joined by one original proponent, blamed the shapes on rock deformation. Both the carbon and the stromatolites remain disputed; the earliest undisputed life is about 3.5–3.48 billion years old.

arch-016.title: The Kaapvaal Craton of South Africa
arch-016.text:
South Africa's gold and diamonds sit on one of the oldest stable slabs of crust anywhere. The Kaapvaal Craton formed and stabilized between 3.7 and 2.6 billion years ago, as batholiths, huge bodies of granite that cooled underground, thickened its crust. With the Pilbara it is one of only two pristine Archean crusts known.

Its oldest parts are tonalitic gneisses of about 3.6–3.7 billion years, joined by granite-greenstone terranes of 3.0–3.5 billion. From 3.0 to 2.7 billion years ago, collisions between the continent and volcanic arcs built basins filled with thick volcanic and sedimentary piles. Its granite is exposed today in the core of the Vredefort impact structure.

arch-019.title: The Wyoming Craton begins
arch-019.text: Beneath the Rocky Mountains lies a block of crust older than almost anything on the continent. The Wyoming Craton began as a 100,000 km² Archean craton with gneisses of 3.6–3.0 billion years. Its rocks reach 3.5 billion years, and detrital zircons in them go back 4.0 billion. Late Archean magmatism and plate movements reworked it, and by the end of the eon its three subprovinces had joined.

arch-018.title: Vaalbara, a first supercontinent?
arch-018.text:
South Africa and Western Australia have rock records that match too well to be chance, or so one hypothesis argues. The Kaapvaal and Pilbara cratons may have joined as Vaalbara, one of Earth's earliest supercontinents, as far back as about 3.6 billion years ago. They show strikingly similar rock sequences from 3.5 to 2.7 billion years ago and share impact spherule layers of 3.5–3.2 billion years.

The case is far from closed. Paleomagnetic data hint at a link even at 3.87 billion years, but an early Vaalbara cannot be proven. By 2.78–2.77 billion years ago the cratons lay 30° of latitude apart, so it had broken up by about 2.8 billion. Some scientists explain the shared features as global processes, and Vaalbara competes with the largely incompatible {{ref:arch-036}} hypothesis.

arch-017.title: India's Dharwar Craton forms
arch-017.text: The oldest part of the Indian peninsula was built by ocean floor sinking and melting. India's Dharwar Craton formed between 3.6 and 2.5 billion years ago. Around 3350 million years ago, ridge push drove oceanic crust down into the mantle, and the melting slab produced its TTG crust of tonalite, trondhjemite and granodiorite, light granite-like rocks. Its three blocks joined between 2560 and 2500 million years ago, closing all of its subduction zones, where one plate dives beneath another.

arch-020.title: The Barberton Greenstone Belt
arch-020.text: Some of Africa's oldest mountains rise on the border of South Africa and Eswatini. Lavas and sediments of the Barberton belt were laid down there between 3.5 and 3.2 billion years ago. The area grew in two episodes of terrane accretion, about 3.5 and 3.2 billion years ago, each matching a pulse of TTG magma. Its Makhonjwa Mountains are among the oldest in Africa, and its rocks hold some of the oldest traces of life.

arch-021.title: Spherule layers record giant impacts
arch-021.text:
Thin beds of glassy beads are all that remain of asteroids that hit the early Earth. These spherules are droplets of rock melted and thrown out by an impact, then rained back down. Spherules 3.5 billion years old in South Africa and Western Australia are the oldest known products of impacts on Earth.

In the Barberton belt, eight spherule layers, named S1 to S8 and about 3.5–3.2 billion years old, record at least four and perhaps eight or more impacts. A 2024 review counts 36 layers, from 3.47–3.22 billion and 2.63–2.49 billion years ago, and reads them as a tail of the Late Heavy Bombardment. The objects were not small: the record from 3.2 billion years includes impacts by bodies up to 100 km wide.

arch-022.title: Dresser stromatolites, the earliest undisputed life
arch-022.text:
In the red hills of Western Australia's Pilbara lies the oldest life no one seriously disputes. Stromatolites in the Dresser Formation, deposited about 3483–3479 million years ago, are the earliest direct evidence of life. Stromatolites are layered mounds built as microbial mats trap sediment, layer upon layer.

The evidence runs deeper than the mounds. Microbially induced sedimentary structures of the same age record microbial mats, the earliest life with good fossil evidence. The formation's North Pole chert, a glassy silica rock, holds microfossils, mat fabrics, and carbon and sulfur signatures that suggest heat-loving microbes.

The setting was hot and wet. The stromatolites grew mostly in a shallow lagoon or flooded caldera, a collapsed volcanic crater, where seawater mixed with hydrothermal fluids. Some formed near hot springs on land, a clue explored in {{ref:arch-023}}. Older claims, such as those at {{ref:arch-015}}, remain disputed. The stromatolite record gives the earliest undisputed evidence of life from at least 3.5 billion years ago.

arch-023.title: Life may reach the land
arch-023.text:
Life on land may be almost as old as life itself. Microbes may have lived on land by 3.48 billion years ago: geyserite, a mineral crust laid down by hot springs, in the Pilbara's Dresser Formation holds possible traces. The veins of one 3.5-billion-year-old hot-spring setting held elements life needs, such as phosphorus, boron, nitrogen and sulfur.

Some evidence of prokaryotes, simple cells without a nucleus, colonizing land predates 3 billion years and may reach back to 3.5 billion. Fossil microbes from land-based mats show life was established on land by 3.22 billion years ago. By at least 2.7 billion years ago microbes had built land ecosystems, with organic-rich soils and ponds recorded by 2,800 million years ago.

arch-024.title: The Apex chert microfossils
arch-024.text: A few dark threads in Australian chert may be the oldest fossils of life, or not fossils at all. The 3.465-billion-year-old Apex chert of the Pilbara may hold permineralized microorganisms, cells turned to stone by minerals. Fossils from the Warrawoona Group were once likened to cyanobacteria, but cyanobacterial fossils this old are considered possible yet questionable. Nearby 3.47-billion-year-old baryte and Mount Ada Basalt hold further possible traces. Whether the Apex structures are biological is contested.

arch-025.title: Strelley Pool stromatolites react to change
arch-025.text: These stromatolites seem to respond to their surroundings, as living communities do. In Western Australia's 3.43-billion-year-old Strelley Pool Formation, they change in ways that suggest microbial communities reacting to shifting conditions. They imply photosynthesis, with or without oxygen, since at least 3.43 billion years ago, and the formation holds diverse microfossil shapes too. A 2009 find gave strong evidence of microbial stromatolites by 3.45 billion years, the oldest life visible to the naked eye.

arch-026.title: Methane microbes beneath Barberton's seafloor
arch-026.text: Life may already have been living underground, below the seafloor. About 3.42 billion years ago, threadlike filaments, possibly of microbes that made or ate methane, lived in a vein system beneath the seabed at Barberton. Nearby, the Buck Reef and Josefsdal cherts hold microbial mats with fossil bacteria, and Kromberg microbes show reproduction by fission, splitting in two. Flat-layered stromatolites occur in the 3.46 Hooggenoeg, 3.42 Kromberg and 3.33-billion-year-old Mendon formations.

arch-027.title: A nitrogen sky with almost no oxygen
arch-027.text:
A visitor to the Archean would have suffocated. By about 3.4 billion years ago, nitrogen was the main gas of a stable second atmosphere that also held methane, carbon dioxide, water vapor and sulfur gases. Volcanic outgassing made it, with extra gases from huge asteroids of the Late Heavy Bombardment.

It was anoxic and weakly reducing. Oxygen stayed around or below 0.001% of today's level until about 2.4 billion years ago, because any oxygen made by early photosynthesis was quickly used up oxidizing iron, sulfur and methane. Sulfur-isotope signals rule out significant oxygen before about 2.45 billion years ago. River and delta grains of pyrite, siderite and uraninite older than 2.4 billion years tell the same story, since these minerals break down in oxygen.

arch-028.title: Granite intrudes at the Johannesburg Dome
arch-028.text: Johannesburg sits on a dome of very old granite. Tonalitic and trondhjemitic magma, both granite-like, intruded dark mafic–ultramafic greenstone in the central Kaapvaal Craton, forming South Africa's Johannesburg Dome. Uranium–lead dating of single zircons gives 3340 ± 3 million years, the oldest granitoid phase recognized there so far. Later mafic dikes and granodiorites, some dated 3121 ± 5 million years, support the view that the craton grew in episodes, piece by piece.

arch-029.title: The Zimbabwe Craton welds together
arch-029.text: Diamonds come from deep roots, and the Zimbabwe Craton has one. Its Tokwe and Rhodesdale segments, with rocks as old as 3.46 billion years, stabilized about 3.3 billion years ago. The craton formed where these two smaller blocks were sutured, or welded, together. With the Kaapvaal Craton and Limpopo Belt, it rests on a buoyant mantle root about 250 km thick that yields diamonds.

arch-030.title: Fig Tree microfossils
arch-030.text: Some of the first creatures ever named are microscopic and 3.26 billion years old. South Africa's Fig Tree Formation, about 3.28–3.22 billion years old, holds stromatolites and fossils of microscopic life from about 3.26 billion years ago. Among its fossils are Archaeosphaeroides barbertonensis and Eobacterium, simple cells preserved in stone from the Archean seafloor.

arch-031.title: The S2 impact, a planet-shaking blow
arch-031.text:
About 3.26 billion years ago, an asteroid about 37–58 km wide hit Earth. The only direct trace is the S2 spherule layer in the Barberton Greenstone Belt, but the scale of the blow is staggering. Its crater may have been almost 480 km across, two and a half times the diameter of Chicxulub's, the crater linked to the dinosaurs' end.

The impact probably shook the whole planet with strong earthquakes. It raised megatsunamis thousands of meters high. Its heat boiled the surface of the sea, evaporating tens of meters of the global ocean. Any microbial mats in the shallows would have felt it.

arch-032.title: Microbial mats on Moodies tidal flats
arch-032.text: Tides were already washing over sand and mud 3.22 billion years ago, and microbes were living on them. The Moodies Group of South Africa and Eswatini, laid down then, holds Earth's oldest well-preserved siliciclastic tidal deposits, made of sand and mud grains. Microbial mats flourished on its tidal flats, and its microfossils are among the few accepted Archean examples. It overlies the {{ref:arch-030}} rocks in the Barberton belt.

arch-034.title: Cyanobacteria learn to make oxygen
arch-034.text:
Every breath you take traces back to a microbe that learned to split water. Evidence of oxygen-producing photosynthesizers appears about 3.2 billion years ago, with local free oxygen around stromatolites on carbonate platforms.

The pioneers were cyanobacteria. They arose in fresh water or on land in the middle Archean. Some claims reach back to 3.5 billion years, and 2026 genetic work considers an origin 2.9–3 billion years ago established. Unlike {{ref:arch-013}}, they split water and released oxygen as waste.

That oxygen did not fill the air at once. It first oxidized iron dissolved in the oceans, forming iron ore. It built up only slowly, poisoning many bacteria, and eventually triggered the Great Oxygenation Event after the Archean. Some evidence once seemed to settle the question early. Pilbara biomarkers of 2.7 billion years were read as signs of cyanobacteria and eukaryotes, but were later shown to be contamination. The timing remains debated.

arch-033.title: A hot world under a methane greenhouse
arch-033.text:
Archean seas may have been hot enough to scald. Oxygen isotopes in Mesoarchean cherts suggest ocean temperatures of about 55–85 °C, though weathering studies suggest averages below 50 °C. Either way, the climate was at least temperate.

High levels of methane and carbon dioxide may explain the warmth. Volcanoes supplied the carbon dioxide and early microbes the methane, which lasted longer in an atmosphere without oxygen. Nitrogen levels were probably similar to today's, so nitrogen did little warming. There was a brake, too: sunlight breaking apart methane may have made an organic haze with a cooling, anti-greenhouse effect.

arch-036.title: Ur, a contested early supercontinent
arch-036.text:
Pieces of India, western Australia and southern Africa may once have been a single landmass. Ur is a hypothetical supercontinent of those rocks, formed around 3.1 billion years ago. Its assembly is put at 3,200–2,600 million years ago, and it would have covered only 12–16% of today's continental crust.

The main argument is that cratons stable by about 3 billion years ago all sat in one region of Pangaea. Rogers proposed that Ur later grew into East Gondwana by joining East Antarctica. But a conflicting hypothesis joins western Australia and southern Africa as {{ref:arch-018}}, and most proposed Archean supercontinents remain controversial.
